title: Proximal Difference-in-Differences for Long-Term Causal Learning under Confounding and Outcome Drift
claim: Treated and control groups diverge after a crossover, leaving the continued-control outcome unobserved; an external control is needed to identify it.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right timeline, three horizontal arms split by dashed crossover line
description: A single wide timeline diagram split by a vertical dashed grey line into a 'Trial period (t = pre)' on the left and an 'Extension period (t = 0)' on the right. Three horizontal arms are labeled at left: 'RCT treated, S=1' (orange, flat line), 'RCT control, S=1' (orange), and 'EC, S=0' (green, flat line). Each arm carries outcome notation such as Y_pre^{1,(1)} before the split and Y_0^{1,(1,1)} after it. At the 'Crossover' point the RCT control arm branches. A solid orange line goes up to the treated trajectory, Y_0^{1,(0,1)}. A dashed orange line goes down to the unobserved continued-control outcome, Y_0^{1,(0,0)}, labeled '(unobserved)'. The green EC arm stays untreated and runs straight across to Y_0^{0,(0,0)}. Arrowheads on the right mark progression over time. The eye goes first to the branching crossover.
caption: \tred{RCT and EC study design: the RCT control arm crosses over to treatment during the OLE, while the EC remains untreated.}
abstract: Estimating long-term treatment effects is essential in regulatory and healthcare decision-making, yet the limited follow-up duration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) poses a significant challenge. Open-label extension studies attempt to capture additional information for treated subjects, but there is often significant systematic censoring and selection bias due to placebo crossover. While supplementing RCTs with real-world evidence is a common strategy, existing methods often rely on restrictive exchangeability assumptions that fail under latent confounding. We propose a novel proximal framework to integrate real-world evidence into an RCT with an open-label extension to estimate the long-term continued-control trajectory. Our approach successfully identifies long-term effects even in the presence of time-varying latent confounding effects and inter-study outcome drift. We provide a doubly robust locally efficient estimator that provides further resilience to model misspecification. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework maintains validity in complex data-generating processes where standard approaches may be biased.
